transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi... yeah, I guess I'm here because I just barely sleep right anymore. It’s like the whole night is just this long, drawn-out ordeal now. I'll just lie there in my bed, staring at the ceiling for hours, and if it's raining—man, even if it's just a little drizzle outside—I hear that rain hitting the window and my brain just goes into overdrive. I start thinking about the bluff, you know? Just picturing the bluff giving way and everything sliding, and I just can't turn my head off no matter what I do. I try to look at my phone or whatever to distract myself, but it doesn't really work. 

And then, when I finally do manage to pass out just from pure exhaustion, it's not even good sleep. I have these dreams, and I'll wake up completely drenched in sweat, like my sheets are just soaked and my heart is pounding. It's happening basically every night, so by the time my alarm actually goes off, I have to drag myself out of bed and show up to my shift at the call center feeling like I never even closed my eyes. And let me tell you, working customer service and having people yell at you on the phone all day when your brain feels like mush because you haven't really slept... it's just getting to be way too much. I can't keep doing it like this.
You mentioned having dreams that leave you drenched in sweat, can you tell me more about what happens in those dreams?

Well, the dreams... yeah, they're always about the bluff. It's like I'm right back there, you know? But the thing is, it's not even just the dreams anymore. That's what's really starting to mess with me. I'll be wide awake, just sitting at my desk at the call center, right? I've got my headset on, I'm trying to help some lady figure out why her bill is five dollars higher this month, and out of absolutely nowhere—I mean, totally unprovoked—stuff just pops into my head. 

Like, I'll suddenly hear this sound. It's this very specific sound of rocks sliding, that kind of grinding, heavy crunching noise. Or I'll get this sudden, vivid feeling like my leg is stuck under me again, pinned down, and I can't move it. And for a minute... man, for a minute, I'm not in that cubicle anymore. I'm not looking at my computer screen. I'm right back on that trail, feeling the dirt and the panic all over again. It's so real, it takes my breath away, and I have to physically shake my head to snap out of it and remember I'm at work. And the lady on the phone is going, "Hello? Hello? Are you still there?" and I'm just sitting there trying to remember how to breathe. It happens when I'm driving, too, or just watching TV. Just... boom. Right back there.
Are these flashbacks or memories of the bluff happening at any specific times or when you're exposed to certain things?

Well, yeah, actually... I mean, I try really hard to make sure I'm not exposed to certain things, you know? Like, I used to go out to the coast trails all the time. Every weekend, basically. It was my whole thing, just getting out of the city, getting away from the phones and the yelling customers. But now? Man, I won't go anywhere near those trails. I won't even drive on the highway that heads out that direction. If I have to go somewhere and the GPS tries to route me that way, I'll literally take a 45-minute detour just so I don't have to see the signs for the state park. 

And it's not just the places, it's... well, it's the guys I used to go with, too. My hiking buddies. They keep texting me, right? Like, "Hey man, we're hitting the ridge this weekend, you in?" or "Haven't seen you in a while, let's go grab a beer and plan a trip." And I just... I dodge them. I leave them on read. I feel terrible about it, because they're good guys and we've been friends since high school, but even just seeing their names pop up on my phone... it makes my chest completely tighten up. Just the thought of having to talk to them, knowing they're gonna bring up hiking, or ask me why I haven't been out, or—God forbid—talk about the bluff... I just can't do it. My heart starts racing, I can't catch my breath, and I just have to toss my phone across the room. So I just avoid them entirely. I haven't seen any of them in months. It's just easier to stay in my apartment, you know? Where it's safe and there's no rocks and no trails.
Do you feel intense fear or anxiety when you think about the bluff or when something reminds you of it?

Yeah, I mean... absolutely. It's not just a little anxiety, it's like this whole full-body reaction, you know? Like, my chest gets incredibly tight, almost like someone is sitting on it, and I can't pull in a full breath. And my heart... man, my heart just starts hammering against my ribs so hard I can hear it in my ears. 

Even if it's just something small, like seeing a commercial on TV for, I don't know, hiking boots or an SUV driving up a mountain road. Just the sight of a rocky cliff on a screen, and suddenly I'm sweating, my hands get all clammy, and I feel this overwhelming panic, like I need to run away right that second. I literally have to change the channel or leave the room. It’s like my brain completely short-circuits. I can't focus on anything else. I'll just be sitting on my couch, totally safe, but my body is reacting like I'm about to get crushed all over again. It’s exhausting, honestly, just feeling that level of terror over a thought or a picture.
How long have you been experiencing these intense fear and anxiety reactions when reminded of the bluff?

Well, it's been... let's see, it's been about four months now. Yeah, four months. It started pretty much right after it happened. You know, after the bluff trail collapsed and I got trapped under all that debris. I mean, at first, when I was in the hospital, I thought maybe I was just shaken up, right? Because, I mean, who wouldn't be? But then I got discharged, and I went back to my apartment, and I thought, okay, I'm safe now, I can just get back to normal. But that's when it really started hitting me. The first time I saw a rock wall on some nature documentary my roommate was watching, and I just completely lost it. And it hasn't stopped since. Every single day for the last four months, just dealing with this constant, exhausting panic every time something even remotely reminds me of being stuck out there. It feels like a lot longer than four months, to be honest with you. It feels like it's been my whole life now, just trying to navigate around all these triggers and memories for a solid four months.
Do you find yourself trying to push away or avoid thoughts about the bluff when they come into your mind?

Well, yeah, I definitely do. I mean, I try really, really hard not to think about it. It's like I was saying before, about the trails and my friends, you know? I just completely avoid anything that might bring it up. I won't go near the coast trails now, not even close. Like I said, I'll take a massive detour just to avoid the highway that goes out there. And I dodge texts from my hiking buddies because even talking about going out there, or just seeing their names and knowing they might bring it up... it makes my chest tighten up so bad. 

But it's not just the physical stuff, it's the thoughts, too. If I'm just sitting there and my mind starts to wander, and I feel that memory creeping in... like, the sound of the rocks shifting or the feeling of the dirt, I immediately have to do something else. I'll turn on the TV really loud, or I'll start scrubbing the kitchen counters, or I'll just put on headphones and blast music until my ears ring. Anything to drown it out. Because if I let myself think about it for even a second, it's like I'm right back under that debris, and I just can't handle it. So, yeah, I push it away. I push it away as hard as I can, every single time it pops into my head, because if I don't, I just spiral completely out of control.
Have you noticed a decrease in interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy before the incident at the bluff?

Well, I mean... I don't know if I'd say I've lost interest, really. It's more just... I don't know, it's complicated, I guess. Like, I still *want* to do things, you know? I still think about the things I used to like doing. Before all this happened, I was always doing something. Like, I'd go to the movies with my friends, or we'd go grab food downtown, or I'd just spend hours playing video games on the weekends. I still like the idea of those things. I don't think my actual *interest* in them has disappeared, if that makes sense. 

It's just that right now, my brain is so preoccupied with everything else. Like, I'm spending so much energy just trying to keep my head above water, trying not to think about the bluff, trying not to have a panic attack when I see a commercial for a jeep. It takes up a lot of mental space, you know? So when it comes to actually doing the things I used to enjoy, I just... I haven't really been doing them, but not because I don't care about them anymore. It's more like I just don't have the bandwidth right now. I'm too exhausted from just trying to get through a normal day at work, dealing with customers and trying to act like I'm totally fine when inside my chest is doing that tight thing I told you about. So by the time I get home, I just kind of crash. But if you're asking if I just don't like those things anymore, or if they don't seem fun to me... no, I wouldn't say that. I just haven't really had the chance to focus on them lately, with everything else going on. I'm sure if things settle down, I'll get back into all of it. I just... I haven't really noticed a drop in how much I *like* those things, just how much I actually *do* them right now.
Do you have trouble remembering certain parts of what happened at the bluff?

Well, honestly... no. I mean, I really, really wish I did. I wish there were parts I couldn't remember, you know? Because... well, it's actually the exact opposite. I remember every single second of it. It's like it's completely burned into my brain. I remember exactly where I put my foot right before the edge gave way. I remember the exact sound it made—it wasn't like a loud crack or anything, it was this weird, deep shifting noise, like a groan almost, right underneath my boots. 

And I remember the smell of the dust when it all came down on top of me. It smelled like... I don't know, like old dirt and salt water mixed together. I remember the exact weight of the debris on my leg, and the color of the sky right before the dust cloud blocked it out. It was this really bright, clear blue, you know, one of those perfect afternoons. I could probably tell you exactly how many rocks were pinning me down if I sat down and drew it out. 

So, no, I don't have any blank spots at all. If anything, my brain just recorded it in, like, ultra-high definition. And it's frustrating because I watch these movies or hear stories about people who go through something crazy and they just black out and wake up in the hospital, and they don't remember the scary part. And I just think, man, how lucky is that? Because I remember every single terrifying second of being trapped there, just waiting and hoping someone would hear me yelling. Every detail, every minute. There's absolutely nothing missing from that day in my head, unfortunately. I remember it all perfectly.
Do you feel guilty or ashamed about what happened at the bluff?

Well, yeah, I do. I mean, it's hard to admit, but... yeah. It's not just a passing thought, either. It's this constant, heavy feeling that just sits with me almost every single day. Under the surface, I just feel... scared. Scared and really, really embarrassed. 

You know, before all this happened, I was always the guy who pushed things to the limit. I was the one leading the hikes, the one who wasn't afraid to get close to the edge, the one who acted like nothing could touch me. I had this whole image, I guess. I was tough. I didn't get rattled. And now... now I'm the guy who got trapped under a rockslide because I was stupid enough to stand on an unstable overhang. I should have known better. I grew up around here, I know how the cliffs are after heavy rain, but I just... I didn't think it would happen to me. 

And now, when I'm at work, dealing with customers or whatever, or even just walking down the street, I have this paranoid feeling that everyone can see it on me. Like they can look at me and just tell that I messed up, that I'm weak, that I'm not the tough guy I always pretended to be. It's like I'm wearing a sign that says "I made a huge mistake and now I'm terrified all the time." It's humiliating. I feel like my friends probably talk about it behind my back, too. Like, "Oh, look at him now, can't even drive past a trail without hyperventilating." I just feel so much shame about the whole thing, like I brought it all on myself and now everyone knows I'm a fraud. It just... it eats at me, you know? Most days, that's just the baseline of how I feel. Scared and totally embarrassed.
Do you try to avoid feeling emotions related to what happened at the bluff?

Well, yeah, absolutely. I mean, I try to avoid anything that even remotely brings up those feelings, because it's just... it's too much. It's not just the feelings, though, it's the places, the people, everything connected to it. Like, I completely refuse to go anywhere near the coast trails now. I used to go out there all the time, right? Like, at least twice a week, rain or shine. But now, just the thought of driving down that stretch of the highway, seeing the ocean on one side and the cliffs on the other... my stomach just drops. I can't do it. I've been taking this ridiculously long detour to get to work just so I don't have to see the water or the bluffs in the distance. It adds like twenty minutes to my commute, but I don't care. It's better than feeling that panic start to rise up in my throat.

And it's not just the places, it's my friends, too. My hiking buddies... we used to be so tight. We had this group chat where we'd plan all our weekend trips, talk about gear, you know, just normal stuff. But now, I just... I dodge their texts. I leave them on read, or I make up some excuse about picking up extra shifts at work. Because even just texting about going out there, even just seeing a message like, "Hey, weather's looking good for a hike this weekend," it makes my chest tighten up so bad I feel like I can't breathe. My heart starts pounding, and I get that same awful, trapped feeling I had under the rocks. So I just avoid them. I feel terrible about it, because they're good guys and they're probably wondering what's wrong with me, but I just can't handle the emotions that come with even talking about it. So yeah, I try to avoid the feelings, the places, the people... basically anything that reminds me of that day, I just push it as far away as I possibly can.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy doing before the incident at the bluff?

Well, no, not really. I mean, the hiking, obviously, I don't do that anymore, like I said. But everything else? No, I still like doing the things I always liked doing. Like, I'm a big gamer, right? I've got this whole setup in my living room, dual monitors, the whole deal. I play a lot of these open-world RPGs, and honestly, I probably play them even more now than I used to. It's a good distraction, you know? I can just put my headset on, get lost in this totally different world for hours, and not have to think about anything else. I'll sit down after a shift at work, and next thing I know, it's 2:00 in the morning and I've just been grinding out quests the whole time. 

And I still like working on my car. I've got this old Honda Civic that I've been slowly fixing up since high school. It's nothing fancy, but I like tinkering with it. Just last weekend, I spent like four hours in the driveway changing out the brake pads and flushing the fluids. It's satisfying, you know, getting your hands dirty and actually fixing a problem you can see and touch. It's straightforward. So yeah, I still enjoy that just as much as I always did. 

And I still watch movies, I still listen to the same music... I don't know, I guess my interests haven't really changed at all. It's just the outdoor stuff, the stuff that involves being near the cliffs or out in nature, that's completely gone. But the inside stuff, the stuff I do at home? That's all still there. If anything, I lean into those hobbies a lot harder now because it's safe. I know exactly what to expect when I boot up a game or pop the hood of my car. There's no surprises. So, no, I haven't lost interest in my hobbies or anything like that. I just... I just stick to the ones that keep me indoors, I guess.
Do you have trouble concentrating on things like work or hobbies since the incident at the bluff?

Concentrating? No, not really. I mean, I haven't really noticed any issues with that. Like I was saying about the video games, right? I can sit there for literally six, seven hours straight, just totally dialed in. I don't lose focus at all. I'm tracking all these different quests, managing my inventory, coordinating with other players online if I'm doing a raid or something... it takes a lot of mental energy to keep all that straight, and I don't miss a beat. If anything, my focus is almost too intense when I'm doing that stuff, because I just want to block everything else out. 

And at work... well, I do customer service, mostly over the phone and some email support. It's not exactly rocket science, but you do have to pay attention to what the person is saying, look up their account, troubleshoot their issue, log the call... there's a whole process to it. And I haven't messed any of that up. I haven't been getting bad reviews from customers or having my manager pull me aside to say I'm making mistakes. I just put my headset on, pull up the CRM software, and just grind through the queue. I can read through a long, complicated email from a frustrated customer and figure out exactly what's wrong with their order without having to read it three times, you know? 

Even with the car stuff... like, when you're doing brakes, you have to be paying attention. You can't just space out when you're putting the calipers back on or bleeding the lines, because if you screw that up, you're going to crash. And I don't have any problem keeping my mind on the task when I'm out there with my tools. It's like, my hands know what to do, and my brain is right there with them. I'm checking the torque specs, making sure everything is aligned perfectly. So, yeah, I don't think my concentration has taken a hit at all. I'm just as sharp with that stuff as I was before. It's just the emotional stuff that's a wreck, but my actual ability to focus on a task? No, that's totally fine. I haven't noticed any change there whatsoever.
Do you find it harder to trust people now than you did before the incident at the bluff?

Trust people? Um... I don't know if it's about trusting *people*, exactly. I mean, my friends didn't cause the rocks to fall, right? And the customers I talk to at work, they're just people with broken routers or whatever. But... I guess it's more about trusting... everything else? Trusting myself, mostly. 

Like, I just keep replaying it in my head, over and over, and I keep thinking about how stupid I was. How incredibly careless I was for being out there alone. I mean, who goes scrambling around unstable cliffs by themselves? It was just so dumb. I should have known better. I grew up around here, I know the coast is dangerous, but I just... I didn't think. And now, because I was so stupid, I have this constant feeling that... well, that I can't trust the world around me. 

It's like, if I let my guard down, even for a second, no matter where I am, something bad is going to happen. It doesn't even have to be at the cliffs. I could be at the grocery store, or just sitting in my living room, and I'll get this sudden thought like, 'What if the roof caves in?' or 'What if someone runs a red light and plows into my car?' It's exhausting. I feel like I always have to be on high alert, always scanning for danger, because the one time I wasn't, the one time I thought I was safe and just enjoying a hike, I ended up pinned under a boulder. So, it's not really that I think people are out to get me or anything. It's just this overwhelming belief that the world is inherently dangerous, and that I'm too careless to navigate it safely, so if I relax for even a moment, I'm going to get crushed again. Literally or figuratively, you know? It just feels like disaster is always waiting right around the corner, just waiting for me to be stupid enough to step into it.
Have you noticed any changes in your relationships with friends or family since the incident at the bluff?

Changes in my relationships? Um, no, not really. I mean, my friends are still my friends, you know? Like, my buddy Mike, for example. We've known each other since, man, probably seventh grade? We still talk pretty much every single day. If anything, we might even talk more now because, like I was saying earlier, I'm playing a lot more games, and he's usually online too. We'll be in a Discord call for like five, six hours on a Saturday night just messing around, running dungeons or whatever we're currently hooked on. He knows all about what happened at the bluff, obviously, but he doesn't treat me any differently, which I really appreciate. We just joke around and give each other a hard time like we always did. And the rest of the guys in our group, it's the exact same. I don't feel disconnected from them or anything like that. 

And my family... well, it's mostly just me and my mom. She worries, obviously. I mean, I guess moms always worry, right? But after I got stuck out there, she was a total wreck for a few weeks. She was calling me constantly, like twice a day, just to make sure I was okay, asking if I was eating, that kind of stuff. But we've always been pretty close anyway. I still go over to her place for dinner on Sundays. She makes this really good pot roast, or sometimes we just order pizza if she's tired from her job, and we just sit and watch TV and catch up. I definitely don't feel like pulling away from her, and she isn't pulling away from me. If anything, she's maybe a little more overbearing now, but not in a bad way. Just in a 'I almost lost my kid' kind of way, which, you know, I totally get. 

So, yeah, I'm still tight with the people I care about. I don't feel like I'm drifting away from anyone or that things are weird between us now. The social side of my life is probably the most normal part of my life right now, to be completely honest. It's just the stuff inside my own head that's messed up. But with other people? No, it's all good. I haven't noticed any bad changes there.
Have you ever felt like you were outside of your body, watching yourself, since the incident at the bluff?

Outside my body? Like... like watching myself from the ceiling or something? No, man, I haven't had anything weird like that happen. Honestly, I kind of wish I could do that sometimes, just to get a break, you know? Just float up and detach from it all and not have to deal with it. But nah, it's actually the exact opposite for me. I feel way too stuck *inside* my body, if that makes any sense. 

Like, I'm hyper-aware of my physical self all the time now. I don't float away or disconnect at all. When my brain starts looping on the bluff and the rocks falling, or when I'm just sitting around and start getting that tense feeling I told you about, I'm just right there in it. I feel how tight my shoulders get, how I'm clenching my jaw, how my muscles are just braced for impact all the time. I'm just very, very grounded in reality, almost to a fault. 

Like right now, sitting here in your office, I'm totally aware of the fabric on this chair, the hum of the air conditioner in the background, the way my shoes feel on the floor... there's no detachment whatsoever. It's just me, in my own skin, dealing with the constant physical tension. Even when I'm playing games for six hours like I was saying, or taking a customer's call, I'm still physically right there. I never lose track of my body. So yeah, no out-of-body movie director stuff for me. I'm just stuck right here on the ground, feeling every single thing.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences intense fear or anxiety in response to reminders of the traumatic event
doctor.question: Do you feel intense fear or anxiety when you think about the bluff or when something reminds you of it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychological distress when exposed to trauma reminders (often coded as S071), which is not present in the provided symptom profile. S074 refers to a persistent negative emotional state rather than one triggered by specific reminders.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean... absolutely. It's not just a little anxiety, it's like this whole full-body reaction, you know? Like, my chest gets incredibly tight, almost like someone is sitting on it, and I can't pull in a full breath. And my heart... man, my heart just starts hammering against my ribs so hard I can hear it in my ears. 

Even if it's just something small, like seeing a commercial on TV for, I don't know, hiking boots or an SUV driving up a mountain road. Just the sight of a rocky cliff on a screen, and suddenly I'm sweating, my hands get all clammy, and I feel this overwhelming panic, like I need to run away right that second. I literally have to change the channel or leave the room. It’s like my brain completely short-circuits. I can't focus on anything else. I'll just be sitting on my couch, totally safe, but my body is reacting like I'm about to get crushed all over again. It’s exhausting, honestly, just feeling that level of terror over a thought or a picture.

doctor.question: How long have you been experiencing these intense fear and anxiety reactions when reminded of the bluff?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about four months, ever since I got trapped after the bluff trail collapsed.
target_item.reason: The doctor is specifically asking how long I have been experiencing these intense fear and anxiety reactions, which maps to the duration of my symptoms.

patient.answer: Well, it's been... let's see, it's been about four months now. Yeah, four months. It started pretty much right after it happened. You know, after the bluff trail collapsed and I got trapped under all that debris. I mean, at first, when I was in the hospital, I thought maybe I was just shaken up, right? Because, I mean, who wouldn't be? But then I got discharged, and I went back to my apartment, and I thought, okay, I'm safe now, I can just get back to normal. But that's when it really started hitting me. The first time I saw a rock wall on some nature documentary my roommate was watching, and I just completely lost it. And it hasn't stopped since. Every single day for the last four months, just dealing with this constant, exhausting panic every time something even remotely reminds me of being stuck out there. It feels like a lot longer than four months, to be honest with you. It feels like it's been my whole life now, just trying to navigate around all these triggers and memories for a solid four months.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient has avoidance behaviors related to thoughts or feelings associated with the bluff
doctor.question: Do you find yourself trying to push away or avoid thoughts about the bluff when they come into your mind?

target_item.name: Trauma_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: I won't go near the coast trails now, and I dodge texts from my hiking buddies because even talking about going out there makes my chest tighten.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoiding or pushing away thoughts about the traumatic event (the bluff). This aligns with the 'Trauma_Avoidance' symptom, which includes avoiding stimuli associated with the trauma, such as thoughts, feelings, or external reminders.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, I definitely do. I mean, I try really, really hard not to think about it. It's like I was saying before, about the trails and my friends, you know? I just completely avoid anything that might bring it up. I won't go near the coast trails now, not even close. Like I said, I'll take a massive detour just to avoid the highway that goes out there. And I dodge texts from my hiking buddies because even talking about going out there, or just seeing their names and knowing they might bring it up... it makes my chest tighten up so bad. 

But it's not just the physical stuff, it's the thoughts, too. If I'm just sitting there and my mind starts to wander, and I feel that memory creeping in... like, the sound of the rocks shifting or the feeling of the dirt, I immediately have to do something else. I'll turn on the TV really loud, or I'll start scrubbing the kitchen counters, or I'll just put on headphones and blast music until my ears ring. Anything to drown it out. Because if I let myself think about it for even a second, it's like I'm right back under that debris, and I just can't handle it. So, yeah, I push it away. I push it away as hard as I can, every single time it pops into my head, because if I don't, I just spiral completely out of control.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient has lost interest in activities they once enjoyed
doctor.question: Have you noticed a decrease in interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy before the incident at the bluff?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a decrease in interest or pleasure in activities previously enjoyed (anhedonia). My symptom profile does not include a specific symptom for decreased interest/pleasure (anhedonia).

patient.answer:
Well, I mean... I don't know if I'd say I've lost interest, really. It's more just... I don't know, it's complicated, I guess. Like, I still *want* to do things, you know? I still think about the things I used to like doing. Before all this happened, I was always doing something. Like, I'd go to the movies with my friends, or we'd go grab food downtown, or I'd just spend hours playing video games on the weekends. I still like the idea of those things. I don't think my actual *interest* in them has disappeared, if that makes sense. 

It's just that right now, my brain is so preoccupied with everything else. Like, I'm spending so much energy just trying to keep my head above water, trying not to think about the bluff, trying not to have a panic attack when I see a commercial for a jeep. It takes up a lot of mental space, you know? So when it comes to actually doing the things I used to enjoy, I just... I haven't really been doing them, but not because I don't care about them anymore. It's more like I just don't have the bandwidth right now. I'm too exhausted from just trying to get through a normal day at work, dealing with customers and trying to act like I'm totally fine when inside my chest is doing that tight thing I told you about. So by the time I get home, I just kind of crash. But if you're asking if I just don't like those things anymore, or if they don't seem fun to me... no, I wouldn't say that. I just haven't really had the chance to focus on them lately, with everything else going on. I'm sure if things settle down, I'll get back into all of it. I just... I haven't really noticed a drop in how much I *like* those things, just how much I actually *do* them right now.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulty recalling important aspects of the traumatic event
doctor.question: Do you have trouble remembering certain parts of what happened at the bluff?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about dissociative amnesia (trouble remembering parts of the traumatic event), which is not listed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, honestly... no. I mean, I really, really wish I did. I wish there were parts I couldn't remember, you know? Because... well, it's actually the exact opposite. I remember every single second of it. It's like it's completely burned into my brain. I remember exactly where I put my foot right before the edge gave way. I remember the exact sound it made—it wasn't like a loud crack or anything, it was this weird, deep shifting noise, like a groan almost, right underneath my boots. 

And I remember the smell of the dust when it all came down on top of me. It smelled like... I don't know, like old dirt and salt water mixed together. I remember the exact weight of the debris on my leg, and the color of the sky right before the dust cloud blocked it out. It was this really bright, clear blue, you know, one of those perfect afternoons. I could probably tell you exactly how many rocks were pinning me down if I sat down and drew it out. 

So, no, I don't have any blank spots at all. If anything, my brain just recorded it in, like, ultra-high definition. And it's frustrating because I watch these movies or hear stories about people who go through something crazy and they just black out and wake up in the hospital, and they don't remember the scary part. And I just think, man, how lucky is that? Because I remember every single terrifying second of being trapped there, just waiting and hoping someone would hear me yelling. Every detail, every minute. There's absolutely nothing missing from that day in my head, unfortunately. I remember it all perfectly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences guilt or shame related to the incident at the bluff
doctor.question: Do you feel guilty or ashamed about what happened at the bluff?

target_item.name: Persistent_Negative_Emotional_State
target_item.manifestation: Most days I feel scared and embarrassed under the surface, like everyone can tell I messed up and I'm not as tough as I used to act.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I feel guilty or ashamed about the traumatic event, which directly relates to experiencing a persistent negative emotional state such as guilt or shame.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, I do. I mean, it's hard to admit, but... yeah. It's not just a passing thought, either. It's this constant, heavy feeling that just sits with me almost every single day. Under the surface, I just feel... scared. Scared and really, really embarrassed. 

You know, before all this happened, I was always the guy who pushed things to the limit. I was the one leading the hikes, the one who wasn't afraid to get close to the edge, the one who acted like nothing could touch me. I had this whole image, I guess. I was tough. I didn't get rattled. And now... now I'm the guy who got trapped under a rockslide because I was stupid enough to stand on an unstable overhang. I should have known better. I grew up around here, I know how the cliffs are after heavy rain, but I just... I didn't think it would happen to me. 

And now, when I'm at work, dealing with customers or whatever, or even just walking down the street, I have this paranoid feeling that everyone can see it on me. Like they can look at me and just tell that I messed up, that I'm weak, that I'm not the tough guy I always pretended to be. It's like I'm wearing a sign that says "I made a huge mistake and now I'm terrified all the time." It's humiliating. I feel like my friends probably talk about it behind my back, too. Like, "Oh, look at him now, can't even drive past a trail without hyperventilating." I just feel so much shame about the whole thing, like I brought it all on myself and now everyone knows I'm a fraud. It just... it eats at me, you know? Most days, that's just the baseline of how I feel. Scared and totally embarrassed.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of avoidance of emotions related to the traumatic event
doctor.question: Do you try to avoid feeling emotions related to what happened at the bluff?

target_item.name: Trauma_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: I won't go near the coast trails now, and I dodge texts from my hiking buddies because even talking about going out there makes my chest tighten.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about efforts to avoid emotions related to the traumatic event, which is a form of internal avoidance and falls under the symptom of trauma avoidance.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, absolutely. I mean, I try to avoid anything that even remotely brings up those feelings, because it's just... it's too much. It's not just the feelings, though, it's the places, the people, everything connected to it. Like, I completely refuse to go anywhere near the coast trails now. I used to go out there all the time, right? Like, at least twice a week, rain or shine. But now, just the thought of driving down that stretch of the highway, seeing the ocean on one side and the cliffs on the other... my stomach just drops. I can't do it. I've been taking this ridiculously long detour to get to work just so I don't have to see the water or the bluffs in the distance. It adds like twenty minutes to my commute, but I don't care. It's better than feeling that panic start to rise up in my throat.

And it's not just the places, it's my friends, too. My hiking buddies... we used to be so tight. We had this group chat where we'd plan all our weekend trips, talk about gear, you know, just normal stuff. But now, I just... I dodge their texts. I leave them on read, or I make up some excuse about picking up extra shifts at work. Because even just texting about going out there, even just seeing a message like, "Hey, weather's looking good for a hike this weekend," it makes my chest tighten up so bad I feel like I can't breathe. My heart starts pounding, and I get that same awful, trapped feeling I had under the rocks. So I just avoid them. I feel terrible about it, because they're good guys and they're probably wondering what's wrong with me, but I just can't handle the emotions that come with even talking about it. So yeah, I try to avoid the feelings, the places, the people... basically anything that reminds me of that day, I just push it as far away as I possibly can.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of marked diminished interest in significant activities
doctor.question: Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy doing before the incident at the bluff?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about diminished interest or participation in significant activities (anhedonia), which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I mean, the hiking, obviously, I don't do that anymore, like I said. But everything else? No, I still like doing the things I always liked doing. Like, I'm a big gamer, right? I've got this whole setup in my living room, dual monitors, the whole deal. I play a lot of these open-world RPGs, and honestly, I probably play them even more now than I used to. It's a good distraction, you know? I can just put my headset on, get lost in this totally different world for hours, and not have to think about anything else. I'll sit down after a shift at work, and next thing I know, it's 2:00 in the morning and I've just been grinding out quests the whole time. 

And I still like working on my car. I've got this old Honda Civic that I've been slowly fixing up since high school. It's nothing fancy, but I like tinkering with it. Just last weekend, I spent like four hours in the driveway changing out the brake pads and flushing the fluids. It's satisfying, you know, getting your hands dirty and actually fixing a problem you can see and touch. It's straightforward. So yeah, I still enjoy that just as much as I always did. 

And I still watch movies, I still listen to the same music... I don't know, I guess my interests haven't really changed at all. It's just the outdoor stuff, the stuff that involves being near the cliffs or out in nature, that's completely gone. But the inside stuff, the stuff I do at home? That's all still there. If anything, I lean into those hobbies a lot harder now because it's safe. I know exactly what to expect when I boot up a game or pop the hood of my car. There's no surprises. So, no, I haven't lost interest in my hobbies or anything like that. I just... I just stick to the ones that keep me indoors, I guess.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulty concentrating
doctor.question: Do you have trouble concentrating on things like work or hobbies since the incident at the bluff?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about concentration difficulties, which is a specific PTSD symptom. This symptom is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Concentrating? No, not really. I mean, I haven't really noticed any issues with that. Like I was saying about the video games, right? I can sit there for literally six, seven hours straight, just totally dialed in. I don't lose focus at all. I'm tracking all these different quests, managing my inventory, coordinating with other players online if I'm doing a raid or something... it takes a lot of mental energy to keep all that straight, and I don't miss a beat. If anything, my focus is almost too intense when I'm doing that stuff, because I just want to block everything else out. 

And at work... well, I do customer service, mostly over the phone and some email support. It's not exactly rocket science, but you do have to pay attention to what the person is saying, look up their account, troubleshoot their issue, log the call... there's a whole process to it. And I haven't messed any of that up. I haven't been getting bad reviews from customers or having my manager pull me aside to say I'm making mistakes. I just put my headset on, pull up the CRM software, and just grind through the queue. I can read through a long, complicated email from a frustrated customer and figure out exactly what's wrong with their order without having to read it three times, you know? 

Even with the car stuff... like, when you're doing brakes, you have to be paying attention. You can't just space out when you're putting the calipers back on or bleeding the lines, because if you screw that up, you're going to crash. And I don't have any problem keeping my mind on the task when I'm out there with my tools. It's like, my hands know what to do, and my brain is right there with them. I'm checking the torque specs, making sure everything is aligned perfectly. So, yeah, I don't think my concentration has taken a hit at all. I'm just as sharp with that stuff as I was before. It's just the emotional stuff that's a wreck, but my actual ability to focus on a task? No, that's totally fine. I haven't noticed any change there whatsoever.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulty trusting others
doctor.question: Do you find it harder to trust people now than you did before the incident at the bluff?

target_item.name: Negative_Beliefs
target_item.manifestation: I keep thinking I was stupid and careless for being out there alone, and now it feels like if I let my guard down anywhere something bad is going to happen.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question about finding it harder to trust people directly asks about negative beliefs or expectations regarding others, which aligns with the Negative_Beliefs symptom.

patient.answer:
Trust people? Um... I don't know if it's about trusting *people*, exactly. I mean, my friends didn't cause the rocks to fall, right? And the customers I talk to at work, they're just people with broken routers or whatever. But... I guess it's more about trusting... everything else? Trusting myself, mostly. 

Like, I just keep replaying it in my head, over and over, and I keep thinking about how stupid I was. How incredibly careless I was for being out there alone. I mean, who goes scrambling around unstable cliffs by themselves? It was just so dumb. I should have known better. I grew up around here, I know the coast is dangerous, but I just... I didn't think. And now, because I was so stupid, I have this constant feeling that... well, that I can't trust the world around me. 

It's like, if I let my guard down, even for a second, no matter where I am, something bad is going to happen. It doesn't even have to be at the cliffs. I could be at the grocery store, or just sitting in my living room, and I'll get this sudden thought like, 'What if the roof caves in?' or 'What if someone runs a red light and plows into my car?' It's exhausting. I feel like I always have to be on high alert, always scanning for danger, because the one time I wasn't, the one time I thought I was safe and just enjoying a hike, I ended up pinned under a boulder. So, it's not really that I think people are out to get me or anything. It's just this overwhelming belief that the world is inherently dangerous, and that I'm too careless to navigate it safely, so if I relax for even a moment, I'm going to get crushed again. Literally or figuratively, you know? It just feels like disaster is always waiting right around the corner, just waiting for me to be stupid enough to step into it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulty maintaining relationships due to their symptoms
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your relationships with friends or family since the incident at the bluff?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in relationships, which typically maps to feelings of detachment or estrangement from others (S071). This symptom is not in my profile.

patient.answer:
Changes in my relationships? Um, no, not really. I mean, my friends are still my friends, you know? Like, my buddy Mike, for example. We've known each other since, man, probably seventh grade? We still talk pretty much every single day. If anything, we might even talk more now because, like I was saying earlier, I'm playing a lot more games, and he's usually online too. We'll be in a Discord call for like five, six hours on a Saturday night just messing around, running dungeons or whatever we're currently hooked on. He knows all about what happened at the bluff, obviously, but he doesn't treat me any differently, which I really appreciate. We just joke around and give each other a hard time like we always did. And the rest of the guys in our group, it's the exact same. I don't feel disconnected from them or anything like that. 

And my family... well, it's mostly just me and my mom. She worries, obviously. I mean, I guess moms always worry, right? But after I got stuck out there, she was a total wreck for a few weeks. She was calling me constantly, like twice a day, just to make sure I was okay, asking if I was eating, that kind of stuff. But we've always been pretty close anyway. I still go over to her place for dinner on Sundays. She makes this really good pot roast, or sometimes we just order pizza if she's tired from her job, and we just sit and watch TV and catch up. I definitely don't feel like pulling away from her, and she isn't pulling away from me. If anything, she's maybe a little more overbearing now, but not in a bad way. Just in a 'I almost lost my kid' kind of way, which, you know, I totally get. 

So, yeah, I'm still tight with the people I care about. I don't feel like I'm drifting away from anyone or that things are weird between us now. The social side of my life is probably the most normal part of my life right now, to be completely honest. It's just the stuff inside my own head that's messed up. But with other people? No, it's all good. I haven't noticed any bad changes there.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any dissociative symptoms
doctor.question: Have you ever felt like you were outside of your body, watching yourself, since the incident at the bluff?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depersonalization (feeling outside of one's body), which is a dissociative symptom. This is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Outside my body? Like... like watching myself from the ceiling or something? No, man, I haven't had anything weird like that happen. Honestly, I kind of wish I could do that sometimes, just to get a break, you know? Just float up and detach from it all and not have to deal with it. But nah, it's actually the exact opposite for me. I feel way too stuck *inside* my body, if that makes any sense. 

Like, I'm hyper-aware of my physical self all the time now. I don't float away or disconnect at all. When my brain starts looping on the bluff and the rocks falling, or when I'm just sitting around and start getting that tense feeling I told you about, I'm just right there in it. I feel how tight my shoulders get, how I'm clenching my jaw, how my muscles are just braced for impact all the time. I'm just very, very grounded in reality, almost to a fault. 

Like right now, sitting here in your office, I'm totally aware of the fabric on this chair, the hum of the air conditioner in the background, the way my shoes feel on the floor... there's no detachment whatsoever. It's just me, in my own skin, dealing with the constant physical tension. Even when I'm playing games for six hours like I was saying, or taking a customer's call, I'm still physically right there. I never lose track of my body. So yeah, no out-of-body movie director stuff for me. I'm just stuck right here on the ground, feeling every single thing.
